turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, August 6. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Here's the thread running through today — the Hormuz de-escalation trade keeps compounding, even as the two sides start fighting over who actually keeps the toll revenue. Brent and WTI are extending yesterday's slide toward $80 and $75 on that story.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Wall Street's record streak just cracked for the first time in days.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It did — the Dow pushed to a fresh record overnight, but the Nasdaq and the Russell both pulled back off Wednesday's highs. First split tape after a run where everything was going up together. And the same tension between spending more and spending smarter shows up in two completely different places today — a Chinese AI lab's new attention mechanism, and the Texas governor freezing the entire data-center interconnection queue in ERCOT pending an audit.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Efficiency versus scale, basically, playing out on three different boards at once.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly. And in the Philippines, the SONA promises from two weeks ago just turned into an actual twenty-four-bill legislative timeline, the same day a weakening storm finally exits Luzon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A lot on deck. Let's start with India.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's a genuinely striking upset out of Bihar state in India — a special election, or bypoll, in the Bankipur constituency. Prashant Kishor's party, Jan Suraaj, just unseated the BJP by about 18,953 votes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does one state bypoll matter nationally?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it ends a 30-year BJP hold on that specific seat, and it lands right in the middle of a youth-led protest movement — they're calling it the "Cockroach movement" — that already forced the state education minister to resign. Turnout was 34.24%, which is modest, but Kishor built his political career as the strategist behind several other parties' wins before running his own outfit, so this is being read as an early proof point that his ground game translates into actual votes, not just headlines.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth watching whether it's a one-off protest vote or the start of something with legs into next year's state elections.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — one seat doesn't reshape Bihar, but it's the kind of result that changes how seriously the other parties take him.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Meanwhile, the Hormuz story just moved from "there's a deal" to "who gets paid."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This is the genuinely new piece. Iran and Oman have moved past the interim framework we talked about yesterday and are now finalizing the actual mechanics — the route coordinates, so inbound Gulf traffic goes through one lane and outbound through the other, and critically, they've agreed to split a transit "service fee" 50-50 between them. That's contingent on the US lifting its blockade on Iranian ports.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A toll. On one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And it's not landing quietly — eight global shipping-lobby groups have formally protested to the UN, arguing the fee violates international transit norms and sets a precedent that other chokepoint states, think Malacca, think Bab-el-Mandeb, could copy. Treasury Secretary Bessent says a deal could land today or tomorrow.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the diplomacy is basically done, and now it's a pricing negotiation.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is exactly why oil kept sliding overnight — the market's treating "there's a mechanism, even a paid one" as more bullish for supply than "there's no mechanism at all."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And that oil move is a good bridge into the tape, because for the first time in about a week, it's not just green across the board.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — yesterday, Wednesday, the S&P, Nasdaq, Dow, and Russell all closed at simultaneous records on AMD's blowout quarter. Overnight, that broke. The Dow pushed to another fresh record, up about half a percent. But the S&P eased back roughly two-tenths of a percent, the Nasdaq dropped closer to 0.8%, and the Russell gave back about six-tenths.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So value and industrials keep climbing, growth and small-caps take a breather.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read. It's a rotation, not a reversal — nothing here says the AI trade is broken, it's more that after four record closes in a row, the market's catching its breath in the names that ran hardest, while the Dow's more diversified, more industrial complexion keeps grinding higher.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's happening with rates and oil underneath that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Ten-Year's easing further, down to around 4.61%, extending Tuesday's move, as the oil slide takes some of the inflation urgency out of the picture. Brent's at $80.31, WTI around $74.79 — both crudes continuing to extend the Hormuz-optimism slide, way off the $100 and $88.55 spike levels we saw two weeks ago. Gold's up about six-tenths of a percent to $4,331, which is a modest, unremarkable move — no fresh flight-to-safety signal there.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So overall: quiet, mixed, first real pause in the record run.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A healthy pause, if anything. Let's get into the earnings that are actually driving some of this dispersion.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Eli Lilly's numbers are hard to overstate.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: They really are. Q2 revenue came in at 23 billion dollars, up 48% year over year. Mounjaro and Zepbound combined did 14.9 billion of that — Zepbound alone did 4.93 billion, up 46%. Reported EPS was 7.94, up 26%; non-GAAP EPS was 8.38, up 33%. And they didn't just beat, they raised — full-year revenue guidance is now 85 to 87 billion, non-GAAP EPS guidance 35.50 to 36.50.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: At this point the GLP-1 franchise alone is basically a mega-cap company's worth of revenue growth sitting inside Lilly.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is, and the guide raise tells you they're not seeing demand plateau even at this scale.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now the other side of the coin — SpaceX's very first earnings report as a public company, post that 85.7 billion dollar IPO.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And it's a genuinely strong quarter on the numbers: revenue of 7.8 billion, up 92% year over year, beating consensus by about a billion dollars. Starlink and connectivity revenue hit 4.3 billion, up 66%, with subscribers doubling year over year to 12 million. AI-compute revenue was up 247%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That sounds like an unambiguous beat. Why did the stock fall as much as 8%, settling around 5% down at $118.14?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two things layered on top of a great quarter. First, capex-spend concerns — the market's asking the same question of SpaceX it's been asking every hyperscaler this earnings season: is the spending converting to cash fast enough. Second, timing — there's a lockup expiration this week worth over 100 billion dollars, with another roughly 900 million shares set to unlock after Q3. That's a lot of paper that can hit the market regardless of how good the quarter was.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So a beat, punished on the same capex-discipline question that's been running through this entire earnings season.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the same mechanism we saw with Meta a week and a half ago — great growth numbers aren't enough on their own anymore, the market wants to see the spending pay off on a visible timeline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Let's go to Japan, where two of the big automakers just raised guidance on the same day.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Honda first — they've raised their fiscal-27 operating-profit forecast to 650 billion yen, about 4.1 billion dollars, up 30% from the prior 500-billion-yen guide. The net-profit guide flips to a 400-billion-yen profit from what had been a 423.9-billion-yen net loss a year ago. Revenue guidance goes up to 24.15 trillion yen. Q1 operating profit itself more than doubled, to 530.8 billion yen from 244.2 billion a year earlier.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's actually driving that turnaround?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Mostly currency — they've revised their planning assumption to 155 yen to the dollar from 145 — plus genuinely strong US hybrid and motorcycle demand. It's not a one-off; it's a real operating improvement layered on top of a currency tailwind.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Toyota's telling a similar story?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Similar shape, different starting point. Toyota raises its fiscal-26 net-profit forecast to 3.25 trillion yen from 3 trillion — still down 15.5% year over year because of Middle East-tension fallout earlier in the year, so this is a partial recovery, not a full one. Operating-profit guidance goes up to 3.4 trillion yen from 3 trillion, revenue guidance to 54 trillion from 51 trillion. Q1 net profit itself jumped 75.6% year over year to 1.477 trillion yen.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Same weak-yen tailwind as Honda?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That, plus something more specific — Toyota's made real progress securing alternative export routes around the Middle East shipping disruption we've been tracking. So part of this guide raise is currency, and part of it is genuine operational resilience, rerouting around a problem rather than just waiting for it to pass.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: China's playing a different card ahead of Xi's expected trip to the US in September.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Beijing announced case-by-case export controls yesterday on drones, drone components, and related technology bound for the United States, plus an outright ban on dealings with six US entities — including Applied DNA Sciences, a firm called Compliance Testing LLC, and the human-rights NGO Human Rights in China.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a fairly targeted list.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is, and that's the point — this isn't a broad tariff retaliation, it's a scalpel. China's commerce ministry has also opened a national-security review into imported printing software and office equipment, and People's Daily ran a piece separately warning Washington over what it calls expanding tech curbs.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Reads like positioning ahead of the summit — building leverage before the two leaders actually sit down.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read across the wires. Meanwhile the Shanghai Composite itself was steady, around 3,878.92 — gold-miner strength offset a pullback in tech, so the equity market isn't treating this as an escalation yet, more as pre-summit choreography.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Alex, you flagged something out of SemiAnalysis this week that I think ties everything else we've talked about together — the efficiency question underneath the AI trade.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This is genuinely one of the more interesting technical pieces I've read in a while, and it's about a Chinese model, Kimi K3, out of a lab called Moonshot AI. The piece is titled, half-jokingly, "Kimi K3, The Manos, The Mythos, The Legendos" — but underneath the joke title is a serious teardown of the model's architecture, specifically something called Kimi Delta Attention, or KDA.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Walk me through what that actually does, at the level we'd care about, not the math.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: As your context gets longer, the memory you need to hold — the KV cache — grows fast, and that's a huge chunk of your actual inference cost. Most efficient designs try to replace expensive full attention entirely with a cheaper, linear kind. Kimi K3 doesn't — it uses a 3-to-1 ratio, three layers of cheap linear attention for every one layer of full, expensive attention.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So it's a hybrid, not a full replacement.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and that's what SemiAnalysis zeroes in on. Even one full-attention layer every four cuts KV-cache and memory use by up to about 75% on long sequences, while preserving the recall pure linear attention tends to lose. Their line: the 3-to-1 ratio is "a confession and an achievement at the same time" — an achievement because it's a real efficiency win, a confession because linear attention alone still can't fully replace the expensive kind.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does that matter to someone thinking about power demand, not just AI research?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a second lever on the electrons-wall question — do efficiency gains blunt total power demand, or just make compute cheaper per unit and pull in more total usage, Jevons paradox in real time. We've talked about hardware efficiency, chips doing more work per megawatt; this is the same tension one layer up, in the software itself. Cheaper inference eases pressure on data-center demand — but it can just as easily accelerate the buildout, because more applications become economically viable to run at scale.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And notable that it's a Chinese lab pulling this off.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the headline underneath the headline — Kimi K3 swept several open-model leaderboards on release, a clear signal the gap between the Chinese open-source frontier and the closed US labs has essentially closed on raw capability. The competitive story isn't just who has the most GPUs anymore, it's who squeezes the most useful work out of the GPUs they have.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Dense piece, worth chewing on rather than skimming.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Attribution where it's due — SemiAnalysis, from their newsletter this week, for anyone who wants the full technical breakdown.

segments.raw: SEGMENT TWO — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And speaking of data-center buildout running into limits — Texas just did something pretty dramatic.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Governor Abbott sent a letter to the Public Utility Commission and to ERCOT ordering a full audit of every single data-center project currently sitting in ERCOT's interconnection process, before any additional ones are allowed to advance.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How big is that queue, actually?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Over 1,800 projects, representing 474 gigawatts. For context, that's more than five times ERCOT's own all-time peak-demand record. The queue had simply gotten enormous, speculative, and largely unscreened.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So what actually stops, mechanically?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: ERCOT has suspended the Batch Zero Large Load classification notifications that were scheduled to go out August 7th — Batch Zero being the centralized study process that replaced the old utility-by-utility interconnection review for anything 75 megawatts or larger. ERCOT now has to go to the PUC's August 20th open meeting and argue for what's called a "good cause exception" just to justify the delay.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's actually in the audit itself?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Power demand, water use, any public financial assistance the project's received, community protections, and — this is the interesting one — ownership. Abbott's directive specifically wants to know who actually owns each project in the queue.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That ownership piece reads like it's about something more than just grid math.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's a live worry across ERCOT and PJM alike about opaque or foreign capital behind speculative interconnection requests — placeholders with no real intention to build. Ownership disclosure is a direct way to screen that out. This escalates from CenterPoint's Batch Zero rollout and the Texas PUC's behind-the-meter colocation order into a full statewide freeze — a governor reaching into interconnection-queue mechanics, not just a rate case.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: PSEG's playing a different angle on the same pressure — getting ahead of PJM's backstop auction rather than getting caught by it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — PSEG CEO Ralph LaRossa said this week that PSEG Power, their unregulated generation arm, has floated data-center power-supply proposals in New Jersey and elsewhere in PJM inside the bilateral-contracting track of PJM's reliability-backstop framework.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does the bilateral track matter versus just waiting for the auction?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because the backstop auction clears at a price PJM sets centrally — utilities that lock in a negotiated, PPA-style bilateral deal early can secure a data-center customer before that clearing price is even set. LaRossa's also continuing talks around existing nuclear output and future nuclear uprates as offtake anchors — selling the most reliable generation on the system first.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And capital's chasing the demand-side answer too — Base Power just raised a huge round.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: $1 billion, Series D, at a 13 billion dollar valuation — up from 4 billion ten months ago, over 2.5 billion raised total. Their new product, Base Core, is a 39.2 kilowatt-hour LFP residential battery with a 12-year life, entering production at Base Factory 1 in Austin.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A home battery — why does that belong in a gigawatt-scale segment?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because capital's now pricing distributed residential batteries as genuine grid-capacity infrastructure, not just backup power. Base claims 500-plus megawatt-hours deployed and 200-plus megawatts in utility deals — aggregated at scale, a real alternative to the gas-turbine capacity utilities are racing to build for data-center load. The Austin-manufactured angle also plays into the tariff story around Chinese LFP cells we flagged with the Lazard cost data — a distinct, fresh capital story on top of that trend.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So today's energy story in one line: Texas hits the brakes on the supply side, PJM utilities race to lock in demand before the auction prices it for them, and capital keeps hedging toward distributed alternatives to both.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Manila turned the SONA promises into an actual work plan today.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: President Marcos convened the fourth LEDAC meeting — that's the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council — at Malacañang this morning, and notably, he held it despite a storm work-suspension order in effect the same day. Twenty-four priority bills got locked in as the Common Legislative Agenda, with a target of passage by the end of June 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's actually on that list?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The headline ones: the Anti-Political Dynasty Law, a Party-List System Reform Act, the Freedom of Information or Right to Information Act, the BRIGHT Act, which amends bank-deposit-secrecy rules, a Travel Tax Abolition bill, EPIRA amendments to abolish the system-loss charge, and a Child Online Safety and Protection Act.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a genuinely ambitious list — dynasty reform and bank-secrecy reform on the same agenda is not a small ask politically.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Worth flagging as fresh, not an SONA recap — this is the mechanism, the actual bill list and the June 2027 deadline, turning the July 27th SONA rhetoric into legislation. Worth watching which of the twenty-four actually move.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the economy — the peso had its best day in weeks.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It closed at 60.751 to the dollar Wednesday, up 41.4 centavos from Tuesday's 61.165 — the strongest since June 18th's 60.567. Two drivers: externally, positive movement in the Qatar-mediated Middle East talks boosted broad emerging-market demand; domestically, a softer-than-expected July inflation print sparked a rally in local fixed income.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A fresh inflation number behind that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The January-through-July average now sits at 5.0% — still above the 2-to-4% target band, but meaningfully below BSP's own 6.4% full-year projection. China Banking Corporation's chief economist, Domini Velasquez, now sees the peso settling near 60 by year-end absent fresh geopolitical shock.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the storm off Ilocos is finally moving on.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tropical Storm Maymay, international name Kujira, weakened to a tropical depression this morning and exited northern Luzon into the Philippine Sea by this afternoon — downgraded to just Signal 1, down from Signal 2 yesterday. PAGASA expects it to weaken into a remnant low as early as tonight. Notably, the LEDAC meeting went ahead despite Metro Manila and twenty-two provinces still under work suspension.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Governance didn't wait for the weather to clear.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It didn't.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — VOCAB OF THE DAY
segments.label: Vocab Of The Day

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Time for today's vocab. Two Mandarin, then two Tagalog, and as always, we're doing this one in the language itself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 我们先说普通话。今天的第一个词是"归根结底。" (Let's start with Mandarin. Today's first word is "guī gēn jié dǐ.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 归根结底是什么意思呢？(What does guī gēn jié dǐ mean?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 归根结底的意思是"说到底"或者"从根本上说"——用来引出一件事情最核心、最本质的结论。这是比较正式的书面语，常见于财经评论和时事分析。(Guī gēn jié dǐ means "at the end of the day" or "when you get down to the root of it" — it's used to introduce the most fundamental conclusion about something. It's a fairly formal, written-register expression, common in financial commentary and current-affairs analysis.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 能不能用今天的深度报道举个例子？(Can you give an example using today's deep-dive story?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 当然可以。比如说："归根结底，Kimi K3的效率提升到底是会减少电力需求，还是会刺激更多算力涌入，现在还不好说。" (Of course. For example: "At the end of the day, whether Kimi K3's efficiency gain will actually reduce power demand, or just draw in even more compute, is still hard to say.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 归根结底跟"总的来说"有什么区别？(What's the difference between guī gēn jié dǐ and "zǒng de lái shuō," generally speaking?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "总的来说"只是笼统总结，语气随意；"归根结底"带有分析的力度，暗示这才是真正的核心。财经报道里更常用后者。("Zǒng de lái shuō" is a loose, casual summary. "Guī gēn jié dǐ" carries more analytical weight — this is the real core underneath. Financial reporting reaches for the latter more often.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 明白了。第二个词是什么？(Got it. What's the second word?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 第二个词是"息息相关。" (The second word is "xī xī xiāng guān.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 这个词听起来是个成语。(That sounds like a four-character idiom.)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 没错，意思是"紧密相连、彼此影响"，通常用在两件事看起来不同、但实际上互相牵连很深的时候。(Correct — it means "closely, intimately connected," and it's usually used when two things look unrelated on the surface but are actually deeply intertwined.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 今天的新闻里能找到例子吗？(Can we find an example in today's news?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 当然。比如："霍尔木兹海峡的过路费谈判，跟全球油价的走势息息相关。" (Of course. For example: "The Hormuz Strait toll-fee negotiations are closely tied to the direction of global oil prices.") 再比如："德州暂停数据中心并网审批，跟整个电网的稳定息息相关。" (Or another example: "Texas pausing data-center interconnection approvals is closely tied to the stability of the whole grid.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 息息相关跟普通的"有关"有什么不一样？(How is xī xī xiāng guān different from the plain word "related to"?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "有关"比较口语化模糊，只说存在某种联系；"息息相关"程度更强，强调密不可分，一方变化另一方必受影响。("Yǒuguān" is casual and vague. "Xī xī xiāng guān" is stronger — it stresses the two are inseparable; if one changes, the other is guaranteed to be affected.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now let's switch to Tagalog. Ngayon, sa Tagalog naman tayo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo. Ang unang salita natin ngayon ay "humupa." (Yes. Our first word today is "humupa.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ano ang ibig sabihin ng humupa? (What does humupa mean?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang humupa ay ibig sabihing bumababa o unti-unting nawawala ang lakas ng isang bagay — bagyo, sakit, o kahit galit. (Humupa means to subside, or for the strength of something — a storm, an illness, even anger — to gradually fade away.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Puwede bang gamitin natin ito sa balitang pangkapaligiran ngayon? (Can we use this in today's weather story?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo naman. Halimbawa: "Humupa na ang bagyong Maymay pagkalabas nito sa Northern Luzon, mula bagyo tungong depresyon tropikal." (For example: "Storm Maymay subsided after it exited Northern Luzon, weakening from a tropical storm into a tropical depression.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ano ang pagkakaiba ng humupa sa humina, na natutunan na natin dati? (What's the difference between humupa and humina, which we already learned before?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang humina ay pangkalahatan — bumaba lang ang lakas, kahit anong bagay. Pero ang humupa ay mas espesipiko — unti-unting nawawala hanggang halos wala na, tulad ng baha o bagyo na humuhupa. (Humina is general — strength just decreased. Humupa is more specific — gradually receding until almost gone, like floodwater or a storm subsiding.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Malinaw na. Ano ang ikalawang salita? (Clear. What's the second word?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang ikalawang salita ay "isulong." (The second word is "isulong.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Isulong — parang may kinalaman ito sa pagpapatuloy ng isang plano? (Isulong — does this have to do with pushing a plan forward?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tama ka. Ang isulong ay ibig sabihing itaguyod o ipagpatuloy nang may sigla ang isang adyenda, panukala, o layunin. (You're right. Isulong means to advance or push forward — with real energy — an agenda, a proposal, or a goal.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Gamitin natin ito sa balitang pampulitika ngayon. (Let's use it in today's political story.)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sige. Halimbawa: "Isinulong ni Pangulong Marcos ang dalawampu't apat na priyoridad na panukalang batas sa ikaapat na pagpupulong ng LEDAC." (Sure. For example: "President Marcos pushed forward twenty-four priority bills at the fourth LEDAC meeting.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May pagkakaiba ba ito sa salitang "itaguyod"? (Is this different from the word "itaguyod," to champion or support?)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Magkatulad, pero ang itaguyod ay tungkol sa pagsuporta habang hinihimok ito ng iba. Ang isulong ay may diin sa personal na paghila nito pasulong. Kaya sa LEDAC, mas angkop ang isulong — si Marcos mismo ang aktibong nagpapatakbo nito. (Similar, but itaguyod is about supporting a proposal as others advance it. Isulong emphasizes personally pulling it forward. So for LEDAC, isulong fits better — Marcos himself is actively driving it.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Perfect — 归根结底, 息息相关, humupa, isulong. Four solid words for today.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's a wonderfully quiet art story out of New York this week — the Met has hung a Leonardo da Vinci with zero announcement.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does a museum quietly hang a Leonardo?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's on loan from Ken Griffin, the Citadel founder — "Madonna of the Yarnwinder," painted around 1505, hanging in Gallery 609. No press release; it was only spotted because an art advisor posted about it on Instagram, and reporting since suggests it's been there since April.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the catch with the attribution?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The wall label credits it to "the master and his studio," not Leonardo alone. Fewer than 20 Leonardo paintings survive worldwide, and this one carries a genuine attribution question — previously shown at the Art Institute of Chicago in 2011 and the Louvre in 2019, but the hedge on the label is real.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the story isn't the painting, it's how it arrived.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly — a billionaire's contested-attribution Leonardo entering a major public museum through the side door, no fanfare picked over the wall text. That restraint is itself the interesting choice.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's a much louder announcement out of the Guggenheim.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Taryn Simon is going to fill the entire rotunda — first time a photography and film artist's been given that honor there. Opens September 18th. The new work, "Father Country I Do Love You," is 42 chapters combining photography, text, video, and sculpture, built over nearly a decade, tracing the real life of an unnamed federal agent who worked as an evidence-collecting middleman.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A big claim for the venue.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The museum's calling it the largest debut of new work in Guggenheim history — and given the venue's track record, that's saying something.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And one closing soon that's worth catching before it's gone.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The National Gallery in London's Zurbarán show — the first major UK exhibition ever devoted to Francisco de Zurbarán, organized with the Louvre and the Art Institute of Chicago — closes August 23rd, and tomorrow's the final pay-what-you-wish Friday evening.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Has it landed with critics?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Swept five-star reviews across the Times, the Standard, and the Guardian; the New York Times called it one of the greatest shows the critic had ever seen. Nearly 50 works spanning altarpieces to austere still lifes — Zurbarán's the painter Spanish golden-age curators keep insisting deserves Velázquez-level recognition and rarely gets it outside Spain, so a show this well-received in London is itself the story.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One more, and this one's happening literally tonight.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The BBC Proms is performing Weber's opera "Oberon" at the Royal Albert Hall tonight — its first-ever Proms performance, remarkably, in the Proms' entire history. Sir Mark Elder's conducting, marking 200 years since Weber's final opera premiered at Covent Garden in 1826, just weeks before Weber died of tuberculosis at 39.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A genuinely rare programming choice, then.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Very rare — if you're near a radio or a stream tonight, it's worth catching precisely because it may not come around again for a while.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Let's get into what people are actually arguing about right now. John Authers at Bloomberg Opinion had two pieces this week that are worth putting side by side.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The first, from Tuesday, is an Occam's-razor argument about the market's record run — don't overthink it, the simplest explanation for the S&P's record highs is the correct one: blowout AI-linked earnings, Palantir up 27 to 30% on its report, strong Amazon and Microsoft cloud numbers, plus falling oil and yields on Hormuz de-escalation hopes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the pushback?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Occam's razor cuts both ways — a market this concentrated in a handful of AI-earnings prints isn't simple, it's fragile. The uncomfortable part: this exact "simple" story flipped sign three weeks ago, when the same market punished AI-capex spending using very similar data.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the second piece is about the Hormuz toll itself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: From Wednesday — his argument is that whatever arrangement emerges over the Strait, which carries something like a fifth of the world's oil and gas, the world effectively pays regardless of whose flag is on the toll booth. A toll fight itself adds cost and keeps tankers waiting, which functions like a shortage even without one. A messy negotiated deal that gets tankers moving, even at a price, may be the realistic ceiling here — not a triumph, but tolerable.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a strikingly resigned argument for a strategic chokepoint.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is — and that's the counter-take. Framing a hostile actor's toll leverage as "steep but payable" risks normalizing extortion of a global chokepoint and sets a precedent other chokepoint states could copy. Declaring this "as good as it gets" also forecloses pressure toward the alternative on the table — an internationalized, non-toll mechanism modeled on how Malacca is governed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two pieces, same columnist, and together they actually frame the whole Hormuz story we've been tracking pretty well — cautious optimism on the market side, real skepticism on the precedent side.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the tension worth sitting with today.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One good thing today, and it's a genuinely large conservation win out of New Zealand.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Five new marine reserves just took effect along New Zealand's Otago coast, covering about 308 square kilometers — protecting yellow-eyed penguins, New Zealand sea lions, albatross, giant kelp forests, and deepwater coral. Together they lift mainland New Zealand's total marine-reserve coverage by roughly 50%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a huge single jump for one region.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It really is, and the way it's being run is the other half of the story — the reserves are collectively named Te Au Roa o Te Rakihouia, and they were co-developed and are now co-managed by New Zealand's Department of Conservation together with the local Kāi Tahu iwi. Nine rangers, drawn from both the government agency and the iwi, are running the day-to-day water monitoring together.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So indigenous guardianship extending from land into ocean, formally and operationally, not just symbolically.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly — real shared authority over daily monitoring, not just a name on a map. A genuinely good note to end on.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Thursday, August 6. We'll see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Take care, and we'll catch you then.
